title: The lost princess
hook: Rebbe Nachman's tale of a viceroy who searches for years for a lost princess

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rebbe Nachman's very narrow bridge. Your line was not afraid at all. Did you take one step? Today, the same rebbe tells a story, the first of his famous tales. Day three hundred three.

Rebbe Nachman didn't only teach. Near the end of his short life he started telling stories. Fairy tales, really: kings and princesses, giants, deserts, enchanted palaces. His followers were puzzled at first. Why is our rebbe telling us bedtime stories? But he told them these stories hid deep things, and his student Nathan wrote them down. The first one is about a king who says one careless sentence in anger, and loses the person he loves most. Today: the lost princess.
screen: `A REBBE TELLS FAIRY TALES.` → `KINGS, GIANTS, PALACES.` → `ONE CARELESS SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the story, in short strokes. A king has a daughter he loves dearly. One day, angry with her, he blurts out: may the not-good take you. The next morning, she's gone. The king is heartbroken. His viceroy, his second-in-command, asks for a servant, a horse and some money, and sets out to find her. He searches for years. At last he finds her, held in a strange palace. She tells him how to free her: choose a place, long for her for a whole year, and on the last day, fast. On the last day, he sees an apple, eats it, and falls into a deep sleep. He fails. She gives him a second chance: this time, don't drink. He finds a spring, drinks, and sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, she's been taken farther away. All that's left is her kerchief, with a message written in her tears: now look for me on a mountain of gold, in a castle of pearl. So he gets up. He keeps searching. The tale follows him through deserts and giants. And its last line is strange: how he freed her, the story doesn't tell. But in the end, he freed her. Breslov teachers read the princess as the Divine Presence in exile, and the viceroy as every person who has lost something holy and is trying to find it again. He isn't a hero because he never fails. He fails twice, badly. He's a hero because the story always says the same thing next: and he kept searching.
screen: `ONE ANGRY SENTENCE.` · `YEARS OF SEARCHING.` · `AN APPLE. A SPRING. SEVENTY YEARS.` · `A MESSAGE WRITTEN IN TEARS.` · then, large: `KEEP SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep searching for one good thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of something good you once had and have lost track of. A friendship. A habit. A sense of wonder. A way of praying. Don't scold yourself for falling asleep on it. The viceroy slept seventy years and still got up. Just ask: where might I look for it now? One place. One small first step. If you pray, you can ask for help finding it. The bell holds the time.
The lost princess. Rebbe Nachman's first tale: a viceroy who fails, sleeps, wakes, and keeps looking until he finds what was lost.
Your line: keep searching. Today, when you notice you've let something good slip, don't give up on it. Take one step back toward it. Day three hundred three.

howItsDone: Rebbe Nachman's thirteen tales, collected as Sippurei Ma'asiyot, are read and studied by Breslov Hasidim and many others, often with commentaries that explain their hidden meanings.

fork.setup: you're the viceroy. you've failed twice and slept seventy years. all that's left is her kerchief. what do you do?
options: go home. you had your chances.
keep searching, toward the mountain of gold.
stay where you are and wait for her to return.
fork.reveal: he gets up and keeps searching. the tale ends: how he freed her isn't told, but in the end he freed her.

original.note: Hebrew: the loss of a king's daughter, the name of Rebbe Nachman's first tale.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fairy tale about a princess.
what it means: a story about losing something precious and refusing to stop looking, even after failing.
what a scholar hears: the first of the Sippurei Ma'asiyot (published 1815, in Hebrew and Yiddish), read by Breslov as the exile of the Shekhinah and the soul's search to restore it.
